summary:
Mission Arestemis is a 3D first-person educational game that turns space mission systems engineering into an interactive experience. Players receive a mission, configure a spacecraft, build a launch vehicle, manage mass, power, data, communications and Δv, verify their design, and simulate the mission from launch to its final objective.

Instead of working only through menus, players explore a functioning space complex, interact with specialists and physically carry mission data between engineering stations. Every major choice has consequences, helping players understand why real space missions require careful engineering trade-offs.
details:
Mission Arestemis puts the player in the role of a young mission director given responsibility for an entire space mission.

The player arrives at the Space Complex Hyperion, meets an engineer and chooses one of several mission scenarios. These include Mars and lunar rovers, Earth-observation and navigation satellites, space telescopes, interplanetary probes and orbital cargo missions.

The player first adapts a spacecraft by selecting power, communications, navigation, propulsion, computing and scientific instruments. Every component affects parameters such as mass, power consumption, data generation, storage, communication capability, scientific value and cost.

The spacecraft design is saved to a physical data cartridge that the player carries to another engineering station, where a launch vehicle is assembled. The complete mission is then checked for launch performance, Δv, power, communications and mission requirements.

If verification succeeds, the player launches the mission and receives a simulation and post-mission report explaining why the design succeeded, partially succeeded or failed.

The goal is not to find one perfect configuration, but to understand how different engineering decisions interact.

What Makes the Project Different

Mission Arestemis combines a mission-design simulator with a first-person 3D environment.

Instead of presenting space engineering as a collection of disconnected menus, the player physically moves through a space complex and follows the mission-development workflow from objective selection to launch.

The physical data-cartridge system connects the different engineering stages and makes the design process part of the game world itself.
